appraisal_events.evidence: Jupien... révéla depuis qu'elle disait que je ne valais pas la corde pour me pendre et que j'avais cherché à lui faire tout le mal possible.
appraisal_events.explanation: Despite her outwardly devoted, pitying manner toward the narrator, Françoise is revealed (via Jupien) to have privately condemned him as worthless and malicious. The narrator himself doubts whether this was her sincere view or said strategically to turn Jupien against him, so the evaluation stays uncertain.

appraisal_events.evidence: je ne pouvais espérer avoir aucun prestige; car elle était aussi riche que le plus riche qui n'eût pas été noble... en faisait entre toutes une sorte de reine. / Je sentais que je lui déplaisais en allant chaque matin au-devant d'elle.
appraisal_events.explanation: The narrator states plainly that he can hope for no prestige with Mme de Guermantes, since her wealth, rank, and fashionable charm already make her a virtual queen, and he senses that his daily pursuit of her displeases her — a comparative diminishment of his own standing against her elevated position.

status_effects.explanation: Françoise's private verdict that he was worthless and had tried to harm her damages how the narrator is judged, even though only he perceives it and its sincerity is left uncertain.

Across the passage the narrator is doubly destabilized: unsettled by the possibility that Françoise secretly resents him, and certain he holds no favor or prestige with Mme de Guermantes, whom he senses he displeases.
She is framed as supremely wealthy, socially fashionable, and queen-like, which is precisely why the narrator feels he can gain no purchase or prestige with her.

ambiguities: Whether Françoise's disparaging remarks reported by Jupien reflect her genuine opinion of the narrator or were said strategically (e.g. to turn Jupien against him, or to keep his daughter from replacing her as servant) is explicitly left unresolved by the narrator himself.
